title: The Farmer's Son
summary: Akbar challenges a poor farmer's son to solve a riddle that baffled his royal tutors. The boy's practical brilliance wins imperial honor.
full_text:
During an imperial inspection of the countryside, Emperor Akbar stopped his royal retinue near a field where a fourteen-year-old peasant boy named Suraj was guiding a pair of oxen along a furrow. Akbar decided to test the youth's intelligence with a riddle that his royal tutors had debated for hours:

'Young farmer! Can you tell me what travels around the world without ever taking a single step?'

Suraj wiped the sweat from his brow, smiled with sparkling eyes, and replied: 'Sire, the sun and the moon travel around the world every day, yet they have no legs! And beside them, the wind and human thoughts circle the earth in an instant without walking.'

Surprised, Akbar asked a second riddle: 'What grows taller the more you take away from it?'

Suraj laughed: 'A pit in the earth, Your Majesty! The more soil you dig out of it, the deeper and taller it becomes!'

Akbar was thoroughly impressed: 'And what is that which belongs to you, yet is used by everyone else far more than by yourself?'

'My name, Sire!' Suraj answered without a heartbeat's hesitation. 'It is my name, yet my neighbors and parents speak it a hundred times a day, while I rarely utter it!'

Akbar turned to Birbal with profound admiration: 'Look at this peasant youth, Birbal! He has never read Persian poetry or studied Greek logic in a palace academy, yet he answers riddles that stumped my court scholars!'

Birbal said with warm affection:

'Sire, nature and honest labor are the greatest universities. A boy who works in the soil observes the sun, the wind, the earth, and human nature every day of his life. His mind is clear, unburdened by empty pretension.

'Hindustan's true greatness resides in the sturdy huts of its farmers, where common sense and sharp wit flourish like wild wheat.'

Akbar rewarded Suraj with a scholarship to the imperial academy in Agra and granted his family tax-free farmland, proving that talent honors neither pedigree nor poverty.
